newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian army, Khmer rebels hold merger talks.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian army, Khmer rebels hold merger talks.

text.p: Cambodian generals and dissident Khmer Rouge commanders met for the first time on Tuesday in a remote guerrilla base to discuss merging their forces and territories, a participant said.

The talks, held in the northwest guerrilla base of Pailin, aim to cement a peace between the government and the Khmer Rouge dissident faction led by Ieng Sary, who broke with hardline rebel leaders last month.
"There are some things left. They could not reach 100 percent agreement," said defence ministry official Em Mara, who took part in the discussions.

"We will try to solve (remaining unspecified problems) day by day," he said by telephone from the northwest city of Battambang. The government flag was flying over Pailin and the second major dissident base at Phnom Malai, he added.
The military working group was formed after a landmark meeting in Thailand on September 5 between co-defence ministers Tea Banh and Tea Chamrath and Ieng Sary.
But the committee's work had been stalled since early last week pending clarification of the legal status of Ieng Sary, foreign minister during Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot's 1975-79 regime.
Ieng Sary and Pol Pot were sentenced to death in absentia for their role in the genocide of more than one million people. Ieng Sary has said he could not be blamed for the "killing fields" rule.
King Norodom Sihanouk signed an amnesty on Saturday for Ieng Sary at the request of co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen, paving the way for Tuesday's meeting.

Em Mara said the talks focussed on the future ranks, positions and salaries of the Khmer Rouge in the government armed forces. The two sides also talked about building roads to link government-held territory with dissident bases.
Military analysts said road builders would have to clear paths through minefields to reach the rebel bases of Pailin and Phnom Malai, both close to the Thai border.

The government official said they had also addressed the important issue of preparing administrative systems for Pailin and Phnom Malai. The concepts of democracy and respect for the rule of law are alien to the Khmer Rouge, analysts said.
"They have raised the government flag in Pailin and Phnom Malai and the (royal) national anthem is played every morning," said Em Mara.

The two sides forged a ceasefire at earlier talks and the dissidents appeared to have dropped demands for autonomy. But the government has accepted Ieng Sary's Democratic National Union Movement, set up on August 15.

In Pailin, armed forces chief of staff General Ke Kim Yan led the government team that included his two senior deputies, Nhek Bun Chhay and Pol Saroeun. Divisional commanders Sok Peap and Ei Chien and Ieng Sary's son, Ieng Vudh led the Khmer Rouge dissident delegation.
The Khmer Rouge signed a U.N.-brokered peace pact in 1991 but later reneged on the accord. It has been fighting the coalition that emerged from general elections in 1993.
